newsitem.title: HONG KONG: IATA disappointed after HK airport talks.
newsitem.headline: IATA disappointed after HK airport talks.

text.p: Airline representatives said they were disappointed and alarmed after two days of talks over proposed fees at Hong Kong's new airport.

International Air Transport Association(IATA) representative and general manager for Northwest Airlines in Hong Kong, Gilbert Chow, said the Airport Authority had done nothing to challenge his estimate that user fees could quadruple at Chek Lap Kok(CLK) making it one of the world's most expensive airports.
"We came out no better than we went in. Clearly there is a lot more of arduous talking still to be done. It's going to be a long haul," Chow told Reuters.

Another IATA representative at the talks, Lim Liang Poh, IATA's manager, Industry Monetary Affairs, Asia/Pacific said he was also disappointed after the fifth round of talks between members of IATA's User Charges Board representing airlines and the Hong Kong Airport Authority.
The latter is the body responsible for setting fees at the new airport which is due to open in April next year.

"The Airport Authority have proposed substantially higher landing and parking charges. However, we have still not received a full charging schedule from the AA, and there are still some areas where they have not provided any indication on what the costs will be. This is very alarming to the airline community as we are still unable to assess the total increases," he said in a statement.
IATA has estimated a fully loaded jumbo jet would have to pay US$ 12,000 every time it landed at CLK. Analysts said the charge at the existing Kai Tak airport is around US$4,000.

IATA and industry groups such as the Orient Airlines Association along with individual airlines such as Cathay Pacific Airways have increasingly voiced fears of much higher user fees which they say will hit not only airlines and their revenue but the travelling public and the Hong Kong economy as a whole.
The IATA statement said members expressed particularly deep concern over the lack of transparency from the authority which has not made the most up to date 1996 business plans available.

"The airlines understand the need to pay for the airport and not burden the taxpayer. However, our research has shown we do not believe there is a need for such high rates. It is impossible for the airlines to analyse the levels without thorough understanding of the AA's most recent business plans and traffic projections, and we are keen to review this information as soon as possible," Lim added.
IATA remains optimistic that a solution can be reached between the two sides at the next round of talks in April, the statement added.
The Airport Authority issued a statement which said it was also looking forward to next month's talks.

"The AA reiterated that charges at the new airport would be fair and reasonable, allow the AA to meet its obligation to operate on prudent commercial principles and would reflect the "user pays" principle and thus avoid the need for a public subsidy, the statement said.

"The AA is developing and managing the new airport on behalf of Hong Kong, which has made a massive investment in the project from the public purse," the authority's corporate development director Clinton Leeks said in the statement.
